tagline.text: A small waterfall and rocky shoreline, a 10-minute climb from Baler's coastal road

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (free entrance, cottage ₱200, tricycle and others extra, per person)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), about 5–7 hours by road

children.text: Diguisit Falls is a small waterfall reached by a climb of under 10 minutes from the roadside in Barangay Zabali, Baler. Entrance is free, and with a rocky shoreline and Diguisit Beach right next to it, it is easy to fit in between surf sessions.

Diguisit Falls lies in the Diguisit area of Barangay Zabali in Baler, Aurora. Head east along the coastal road from Baler town and the jump-off appears right beside the road, on the right as you come from town. Across the road there are cottages and tables for rent, and on Google Maps the falls are marked between Dragonfly Resort and Sea Grace Villas.

The climb to the falls is short and easy, and it is described as taking less than 10 minutes. Entrance is free, and a cottage rental is reported at about ₱200. It is not a large waterfall, but it is close to town, so people drop in casually. Some accounts add that the upper second and third levels need a short, muddy climb.

Diguisit is not just a waterfall. The beach and rocky coast are close together, which makes it an easy single stop. A few meters from the falls, Diguisit Beach has the Aniao rock formations and the Lukso-Lukso (Diguisit) islets. It is a rocky shore rather than a sandy beach, so it feels different from Baler's other beaches, and at low tide you can reportedly walk out toward the small rock islets. For that reason the place is more about photography and watching the sunrise than swimming. Wikipedia also lists the rocky islets in Diguisit Bay among Baler's sights.

Note that the information in these accounts is a few years old, so fees and trail conditions may have changed. One source gives the Diguisit Beach entrance as ₱20, while another says it is free if you do not go through a resort. Confirm locally. Farther along the same coast are Dicasalarin Cove, managed by Costa Pacifica Resort, and the viewpoint toward the PAG-ASA radar station, so you can surf in the morning and build a half-day route along this road in the afternoon. Baler is a plain-side town at the south end of the bay, about

from Manila by road, and on August 6, 2023 Republic Act No. 11957 officially recognized it as the "Birthplace of Philippine Surfing." American surfer Steve Scott visited in the 1970s and helped make it known as a surf destination, and the cast and crew of the film Apocalypse Now (1979 according to Wikipedia) are also said to have surfed here. That is why many visitors combine a Diguisit trip with their surf trip.

You step out of the vehicle and start climbing right away, so access is easy. Across from the jump-off there are cottages and tables, which is a good place to rest and leave your bags. Entrance is reported to be free.

blocks.title: A short climb of under 10 minutes

children.text: The climb is short and easy, but reviewers warn that it becomes slippery in the afternoon after drenched visitors have passed through. Go in the morning and wear shoes with grip rather than sandals.
The Aniao rock formations lie a few meters from the falls. The shoreline is made of rocks rather than sand, and at low tide you can reportedly walk out to the Lukso-Lukso islets.
Accounts recommend waking early for the sunrise at Diguisit if you stay more than one night. The coast faces the sea to the east, so it is a good place to watch the sun come up.
Experienced climbers are said to be able to test their skills on the rocks. Get permission from your guide or resort staff first, and bring extra safety gear.

Dicasalarin Cove, at the end of the road after Diguisit Beach, is a private beach that requires advance registration. Entrance is ₱300, or ₱100 for Costa Pacifica guests. Opening hours are 8:00–17:00.
Ermita Hill in Baler town is described as the refuge of six families during the 1735 tidal wave. Entrance is about ₱15, and the fees are said to fund scholarships for students at a nearby college.

Back in town from Diguisit you will find the San Luis Obispo de Tolosa Church, the Manuel L. Quezon monument, the Quezon house and the Museo de Baler. The church was the site of the Siege of Baler, which ran from June 1898 to June 2 of the following year. Every June 30 is observed as Philippine–Spanish Friendship Day.

items.title: Half day between surf sessions
items.subtitle: The falls and the rocky coast

children.text: To catch the sunrise, head out early to Diguisit Beach. The rocks are slippery, so wear thick-soled shoes.
Have breakfast at your lodging near Sabang Beach in Baler and take a surf lesson. A board rental with an instructor is about ₱350 per hour.
Take a tricycle to the Diguisit Falls jump-off and climb the short slope, under 10 minutes, to see the falls.
Rest and have lunch at a cottage (about ₱200).
Walk to Diguisit Beach and look at the rock formations and the islets. Check that the tide is out.
Accounts say the climb to the falls is more slippery in the afternoon, so if possible climb to the falls in the morning and visit the beach in the afternoon.

items.title: A full day along the coast road
items.subtitle: Diguisit and Dicasalarin

children.text: Arrange a half-day tricycle tour from your lodging (about ₱300, for three people).
See Diguisit Falls and the beach.
Register at Costa Pacifica, then take a habal-habal (round trip about ₱200–300) up to Dicasalarin Cove.
Return to Baler town and look around Ermita Hill or the town museum.
The road to Dicasalarin is steep and winding, so tricycles cannot go up.
From Cubao in Manila, Genesis buses to Baler are said to cost about ₱550 for 6–7 hours, and Joybus about ₱750 for 5–6 hours. Fares can change, so confirm at the terminal.
By car it is about 230–268 km from Manila and takes 5–6 hours. You use the Manila–Cabanatuan–Baler road.
Aurora has no airport. The nearest international airports are Clark and Manila.
A tricycle is the easiest way. A half-day tour is quoted at about ₱300 and a full day at about ₱800, both for three people.
You can also rent a motorbike for about ₱800 a day or a bicycle for about ₱35 an hour. The coastal road has ups and downs.
On the way to the end of the road, some sections can only be reached by habal-habal (motorcycle taxi).
Rates are from accounts, so bargain and confirm on the spot.
SeaSta Beach Resort runs a boat from Baler Fishport, and the trip is said to take more than an hour. The boat does not dock but floats in Dicasalarin Bay for photos.

A water sports operator at the fishport is reported to charge ₱550 for the Flying Fish (4–5 people), ₱350 for the UFO couch (6–7 people), ₱250 for the banana boat (6–10 people), and ₱1,000 per ride for the Torpedo and the Jumbo (2–3 people). It is open 8:30–17:00.
Sea rates and operations change with the weather, so ask the operator directly.

Baler is a wet place with about 3,357 mm of rain a year, and September–December are the wettest months. August and February are relatively dry. The climb to the falls is slippery in the rain, and waves along the coast can get rough.

The surf season is October–April, and if you visit Baler in this period you can surf in the morning and see Diguisit Falls and the beach in the afternoon. Sunrise is the time when you feel the advantage of the east-facing coast most.
Baler's average daytime high is about
and the nightly low about
, with humidity around 85%. You sweat a lot on the climb to the falls, so bring a change of clothes and water. The rocky coast reflects strong sunlight, so a hat and sunglasses help.

Around Diguisit there are places to stay such as Dragonfly Resort and Sea Grace Villas, but most lodging clusters around Sabang Beach. Accounts often recommend Costa Pacifica, Playa Azul, Blue Coco Baler Beach House and Nalu Surf Camp. Camping ranges from free to about ₱500 depending on the resort, and beach cottages are ₱300–500.

You eat in Baler town. Bayler View is a restaurant overlooking Sabang Beach, and Kubli Bistro is a popular restaurant in the Poblacion. Street vendors sell snacks such as kwek-kwek and isaw, and Suman de Baler, a local specialty of Aurora, is also available. Opening hours can change, so check.

Baler is a small town, so rooms fill up quickly on weekends, holidays and in summer. Accounts advise booking before you arrive and using weekdays if possible. Some accounts say every visitor must pay a ₱100 per person sustainable tourism development fee (SEDF), but this is unconfirmed, so ask your lodging or the tourism office. Bakeshops are noted for brazo de mercedes, yema swirl and asado buns.
Go to the falls in the morning and to the beach at low tide.
Rocks and coral are sharp, so wear thick-soled shoes.
ATMs are scarce, so carry plenty of cash.
Bring a power bank for your phone.
Do not leave your belongings unattended on the beach.
Cottage rates and entry arrangements may require bargaining, so ask ahead.
Carry your trash out with you.
To avoid missing the last bus to Manila, finish your final activity early. There is reportedly a 2 PM Genesis bus to Manila.
Both the climb to the falls and the coastal rocks are slippery and sharp. Be especially careful in the afternoon and after rain, and go to the rock islets only at low tide.
Rocks and coral are sharp, so going barefoot or in flip-flops is risky.
Check the tide times and take care not to be swept off the rocks by waves.
Rock climbing only after getting permission from your guide or the resort.
Dicasalarin requires advance registration and the road is steep, so follow the instructions of your habal-habal driver.
Fees and access arrangements differ between accounts, so confirm them locally.
Use sunscreen that is gentle on coral (free of oxybenzone and similar ingredients) and do not leave any trash behind.
